reverse-nodes-in-k-group.d: Reverse the list's nodes in groups of k; a final group with fewer than k nodes stays as is.
reverse-nodes-in-k-group.i: Loop: find the kth node from the current group start (stop if missing). Detach the group, reverse it, and reconnect the previous group's tail to the new head and the old head (now the tail) to the next group.

reverse-string.d: Reverse a char array in place.
reverse-string.i: Swap from both ends moving inward.

rising-temperature.d: Return ids of days that were warmer than the previous calendar day.
rising-temperature.ex: 2015-01-02 at 25 after 10 the day before -> included
rising-temperature.i: Self-join Weather on DATEDIFF(w2.recordDate, w1.recordDate) = 1 and compare temperatures. Don't compare ids, since dates may not be consecutive ids. LAG() is another option.

roman-to-integer.d: Convert a Roman numeral to an integer.
roman-to-integer.i: Scan left to right: if a symbol is smaller than the one after it (IV, IX, XL, ...), subtract it; otherwise add it.
k: Subtract when smaller than the next symbol
Lookup table for the six two-letter exceptions

rotate-array.d: Rotate an array to the right by k steps, in place if possible.
rotate-array.i: k %= n, then three reversals: whole array, first k, last n-k. O(1) space.
k: Temp buffer for the last k elements

rotate-image.d: Rotate an n x n matrix 90 degrees clockwise, in place.
rotate-image.i: Clockwise rotation = transpose (swap m[i][j] with m[j][i] for j > i), then reverse each row.
k: Copy into a new matrix (not in place)

rotting-oranges.d: Each minute, fresh oranges next to rotten ones rot. Return the minutes until none are fresh, or -1 if some never rot.
rotting-oranges.i: Multi-source BFS: put every initially rotten orange in the queue at time 0. Each BFS layer is one minute. Count fresh oranges and compare with how many got rotted.
k: Multi-source BFS with time stored in the queue

same-tree.d: Return whether two binary trees are structurally identical with equal values.
same-tree.i: Both null -> true; one null or values differ -> false; otherwise recurse on left and right.

search-a-2d-matrix.d: Search a matrix whose rows are sorted and each row starts after the previous row ends. Must be O(log(m*n)).
search-a-2d-matrix.i: Treat it as one sorted array of length m*n: index k maps to row k / cols and column k % cols. Run a single binary search.
k: One binary search over flattened indices

search-in-rotated-sorted-array.d: Search a rotated sorted array of distinct values for target in O(log n).
search-in-rotated-sorted-array.i: One half around mid is always sorted. Check whether target lies inside the sorted half's range; if so search there, else search the other half.
k: Binary search choosing the sorted half

search-in-rotated-sorted-array-ii.d: Same as Search in Rotated Sorted Array but with duplicates; return true or false.
search-in-rotated-sorted-array-ii.i: When nums[lo] == nums[mid] == nums[hi] you can't tell which half is sorted, so shrink both ends by one. The worst case degrades to O(n).
k: Rotated search + shrink on equal ends

search-insert-position.d: Return target's index in a sorted array, or the index where it would be inserted.
search-insert-position.i: This is the lower bound: the first index with nums[i] >= target. Binary search, recording mid whenever nums[mid] >= target.

second-highest-salary.d: Return the second highest distinct salary, or NULL if there isn't one.
second-highest-salary.i: MAX(salary) WHERE salary < (SELECT MAX(salary)). An aggregate over zero rows returns NULL automatically.

serialize-and-deserialize-binary-tree.d: Design serialize(tree) -> string and deserialize(string) -> tree for any binary tree.
serialize-and-deserialize-binary-tree.i: Level-order: write values with a null marker for missing children. To rebuild, read tokens in pairs (left, right) for each node polled from a queue. Pre-order DFS with null markers also works.

set-matrix-zeroes.d: If a cell is 0, set its whole row and column to 0, in place.
set-matrix-zeroes.i: O(m+n) space: separate row and column flag arrays. O(1) space: use the first row and first column as the flags, plus one extra variable for column 0, and fill them in last.
k: First row/column as markers + col0 flag

shortest-common-supersequence.d: Return the shortest string that has both str1 and str2 as subsequences.
shortest-common-supersequence.i: Build the LCS table, then walk back from (n, m): on a match emit the character once; otherwise emit the character from the side you step away from. Add leftovers and reverse. Length = n + m - LCS.
k: LCS table + backtrack to build string

shortest-path-in-binary-matrix.d: Return the length of the shortest path of 0-cells from top-left to bottom-right, moving in 8 directions, or -1.
shortest-path-in-binary-matrix.i: Unweighted shortest path means BFS. The first time you reach a cell is its shortest distance. Check that the start and end cells are 0.

single-element-in-a-sorted-array.d: In a sorted array where every value appears twice except one, find the single value in O(log n).
single-element-in-a-sorted-array.i: Before the single element, pairs start at even indices; after it, at odd ones. At mid, check which side of the pairing you're on and discard that half.

single-number.d: Every element appears twice except one. Find it in O(n) time and O(1) space.
single-number.i: XOR everything: x ^ x = 0 and x ^ 0 = x, so pairs cancel and the single value remains.

single-number-iii.d: Exactly two elements appear once and all others twice. Find the two, in O(n) time and O(1) space.
single-number-iii.i: XOR all gives a ^ b (non-zero). Isolate any set bit (x & -x); it separates a from b. XOR each group separately to get each number.
k: XOR all + split by lowest set bit
